title: How to Pay International Suppliers From Nigeria in 2026: The Complete Business Guide
summary: Paying overseas suppliers from Nigeria means navigating FX costs, CBN requirements, and slow bank transfers. Here is the complete guide to doing it faster, cheaper, and with full compliance.

### CBN Requirements for Paying International Suppliers From Nigeria


Before choosing a payment method, understand the compliance layer. The CBN regulates all outbound foreign currency payments from Nigerian businesses. Getting the documentation wrong delays the payment and in some cases triggers an enforcement review.


**Form A** is the[CBN](https://cbn.gov.ng/) application form required for all outbound foreign currency payments above the applicable threshold. It is submitted through an authorized dealer bank and must be supported by:


- A commercial invoice from the overseas supplier consistent with the payment amount and reference.
- A pro forma invoice for goods not yet shipped.
- For import payments: Form M registered with the Nigerian Customs Service for goods imports above USD 500.
- Bill of lading or airway bill confirming shipment where goods have already been dispatched.
- Packing list and certificate of origin where applicable.


The documentation must be internally consistent. The supplier name, invoice amount, and goods description on the commercial invoice must match the Form M and the payment instruction exactly. Any discrepancy triggers a compliance hold at the bank, which can delay the payment by days and in some cases require the process to restart.


CBN Form A requirements apply to payments exceeding USD 5,000 for Nigerian businesses making international supplier payments.


Using a[CBN-licensed payment platform](https://cbn.gov.ng/) that guides you through documentation requirements at the point of payment initiation, rather than flagging errors after submission, is the single most effective way to prevent compliance-triggered delays.


### The Five Methods for Paying International Suppliers From Nigeria


#####
Method 1: Bank Wire Transfer (SWIFT)


The most common method and the most expensive. Your bank initiates a SWIFT transfer that routes through one or more correspondent banks before reaching your supplier’s bank.


**Cost:** USD 25 to USD 50 wire fee plus 1 to 4% FX markup plus intermediary bank deductions that reduce the amount received.
**Speed:** Three to five business days, longer on corridors with multiple correspondent hops.
**Best for:** Situations where your bank insists on it or for very large transactions where institutional backing matters.
**Limitation:** SWIFT transfers from Africa often route through two to three correspondent banks, each taking a fee. The amount your supplier receives is consistently less than the amount you sent.


#####
Method 2: Fintech Payment Platform


The fastest-growing method for Nigerian business-to-supplier payments. Platforms like Duplo use local banking networks and pre-funded accounts in destination markets to move money faster and at lower cost than the SWIFT correspondent chain.


**Cost:** 1 to 3% all-in, with the full cost disclosed before confirmation.
**Speed:** Same-day to next-day on major corridors. Significantly faster than bank wire transfers.
**Best for:** Regular supplier payments across major trade corridors including China, UK, Europe, UAE, and the United States.
**Limitation:** Coverage varies by platform. Confirm the specific corridor is supported before initiating.


#####
Method 3: Multi-Currency Wallet With Direct Payment


[Hold USD, EUR, or GBP in a multi-currency walle](https://tryduplo.com/blog/how-to-hold-send-and-receive-in-dollars-euros-and-pounds-as-a-nigerian-business/) t and pay suppliers directly from the relevant balance without triggering a naira conversion on every transaction. This is the most cost-effective approach for businesses with regular import volumes in the same currencies.


**Cost:** Near zero on the payment leg when paying from a matching currency balance. FX cost only applies at the point of conversion into the wallet, which you control for timing.
**Speed:** Same-day on supported corridors.
**Best for:** Importers who also receive foreign currency from export customers, or businesses making frequent payments in the same currency.


#####
Method 4: Letter of Credit


A bank guarantee of payment issued to your supplier once specific shipping documentation is presented. Primarily used for large, high-value transactions with new supplier relationships where trust has not yet been established.


**Cost:** 1 to 3% of transaction value plus bank fees.
**Speed:** Five to fourteen days.
**Best for:** First-time orders above USD 100,000 where the supplier requires payment security before shipping.
**Limitation:** Administratively complex and expensive relative to the alternatives. Not suitable for regular, recurring supplier payments.


#####
Method 5: PAPSS for Intra-African Supplier Payments


For Nigerian businesses paying suppliers in other African countries, the[Pan-African Payment and Settlement System](http://papss.com/) enables real-time settlement in local currencies, eliminating the USD conversion cost that applies to all other methods.


**Cost:** Up to 50% lower than USD-routed alternatives on supported corridors.
**Speed:** Near-instant on connected corridors.
**Best for:** Nigerian businesses with suppliers in Ghana, Kenya, South Africa, and other PAPSS-connected African markets.
**Limitation:** Coverage is expanding but not yet universal across all African corridors. PAPSS signed a new settlement bank agreement with Stanbic IBTC Bank in Nigeria in May 2026, extending local-currency intra-African trade settlement for Nigerian businesses.

### A Step-by-Step Guide to Paying an International Supplier From Nigeria


**Step 1: Confirm the payment currency with your supplier.** **** Ask whether they prefer USD, EUR, GBP, or their local currency. Paying in their preferred currency removes friction on their side and may result in a better price or faster shipment.


**Step 2: Prepare your CBN documentation.** **** Gather the commercial invoice, Form M where applicable, and any shipping documentation required. Ensure all figures and names are consistent across documents before initiating the payment.


**Step 3: Choose your payment method.** For regular supplier payments on major corridors, a CBN-licensed fintech platform with[transparent FX pricing](https://tryduplo.com/hidden-fees-international-payments-nigeria/) is the most cost-effective option. For intra-African payments, check PAPSS coverage first.


**Step 4: Check the all-in cost before confirming.** **** Compare the exchange rate offered against the live interbank rate. The difference is your FX margin. Add the stated transaction fee. That total is your all-in cost. Never confirm a payment without knowing this figure.


**Step 5: Initiate and track the payment.** **** A modern payment platform provides real-time tracking from initiation to delivery. Know when funds arrive and share confirmation with your supplier before they follow up.


**Step 6: Reconcile against the purchase order.** **** Match the confirmed payment against the corresponding purchase order or invoice and update your records. With auto reconciliation, this happens automatically.

### Frequently Asked Questions


**How do I pay an overseas supplier from Nigeria?** **** The most cost-effective method for regular payments is a CBN-licensed fintech payment platform that supports direct international payments in your supplier’s currency with transparent FX pricing. For intra-African payments, PAPSS-connected platforms offer the lowest cost and fastest settlement. Bank wire transfers remain an option but carry the highest all-in cost of any method.


**What documents do I need to pay international suppliers from Nigeria?** **** Standard requirements include a commercial invoice from the supplier, Form A submitted through your authorized dealer bank, Form M registered with Nigerian Customs for goods imports above USD 500, and shipping documentation including bill of lading or airway bill where goods have already been dispatched. All documents must be internally consistent.


**What is Form A in Nigeria?** **** Form A is the CBN application form required for outbound foreign currency payments from Nigerian businesses. It is submitted through an authorized dealer bank and must be supported by trade documentation including a commercial invoice and, for import payments, Form M. It applies to payments above the CBN’s applicable threshold.


**How long does it take to pay an international supplier from Nigeria?** **** Bank wire transfers take three to five business days on most corridors. CBN-licensed fintech platforms using local banking networks and pre-funded destination accounts can settle same-day to next-day on major corridors. PAPSS transfers between connected African countries settle near-instantly.


**What is the cheapest way to pay international suppliers from Nigeria?** **** For businesses with regular import volumes in the same foreign currency, holding that currency in a multi-currency wallet and paying suppliers directly from the balance is the lowest-cost approach, as it eliminates the FX conversion cost on the payment leg entirely. For businesses without existing foreign currency balances, a CBN-licensed fintech platform with transparent FX pricing and low all-in costs is the most cost-effective alternative to bank wire transfers.
